tagline: A prophet of Josiah's day announces the great Day of the LORD against Judah and the nations, then sings of a humble remnant and a God who rejoices over his people.
overview:
Zephaniah opens with some of the most sweeping words of judgment in the Bible. God will sweep away everything from the face of the earth, beginning with Judah and Jerusalem, where people worship Baal and the stars, swear by the LORD and by other gods, and say in their complacency that the LORD will do nothing. The great Day of the LORD is near: a day of wrath, trouble, darkness, and trumpet blast. The prophet calls the humble of the land to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility before that day arrives.

The book then widens its view to the nations on every side of Judah (Philistia to the west, Moab and Ammon to the east, Cush to the south, and Assyria to the north) and announces judgment on each. It returns to Jerusalem, the rebellious city whose leaders are like lions and wolves, and whose God is righteous within her. Then the tone changes completely. God promises to purify the lips of the peoples so that all may call on his name, to leave a meek and humble remnant in Zion, and to rejoice over his people with singing.

Zephaniah matters because it holds together the severity and the tenderness of God more tightly than almost any other book. Its Day of the LORD passage gave the church the medieval hymn Dies irae, and its closing song has become one of the most loved pictures of God's delight in his people.
author: The book names its author as Zephaniah, son of Cushi, son of Gedaliah, son of Amariah, son of Hezekiah (1:1). The four-generation genealogy is unusually long for a prophet, and many scholars think it was given to show that the Hezekiah at its head was King Hezekiah of Judah, which would make Zephaniah a distant member of the royal family. The text does not call this Hezekiah king, however, and others think the genealogy may simply trace a family line or explain the name Cushi. The name Zephaniah means the LORD has hidden or protected. Most scholars accept that the core of the book comes from the prophet, though some think parts of the hopeful conclusion were added or expanded after the exile.
date: The heading places Zephaniah in the days of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned about 640 to 609 BC. Within that reign, the book's description of open Baal worship, astral worship, and priests of foreign gods in Jerusalem suggests a time before or early in Josiah's reform, which 2 Kings dates to his eighteenth year (about 622 BC) and 2 Chronicles begins earlier, in his twelfth year (about 628 BC). The oracle against Assyria (2:13-15) speaks of Nineveh's destruction as still future, so the book comes before 612 BC. Most scholars date it to about 630 to 620 BC; a minority place it later in Josiah's reign.
setting: Josiah came to the throne as a boy of eight after the assassination of his father Amon (2 Kings 21:23-24; 22:1). His grandfather Manasseh had reigned for fifty-five years as a loyal vassal of Assyria, and 2 Kings describes his reign as the low point of Judah's worship, with altars to the host of heaven in the temple courts and the sacrifice of children. By Josiah's time, Assyria's grip was weakening; its last great king, Ashurbanipal, died in the 630s or 620s BC, and Babylon was rising. In this space Josiah launched a thorough reform: he purged idolatrous priests and shrines, repaired the temple, and renewed the covenant after the Book of the Law was found (2 Kings 22 to 23). Zephaniah's words fit the religious situation that reform was meant to address, and some scholars think his preaching helped prepare for it.
purpose: Zephaniah was written to warn Judah that its idolatry, injustice, and complacency would bring the Day of the LORD upon it, and to call the humble to seek God before that day. It also shows that God's judgment reaches all nations, and that beyond judgment lies a purified people, drawn from Israel and the nations, who will call on the LORD's name together. For readers after the exile, it explained why Jerusalem fell and held out the promise of a restored and rejoicing Zion.
story: Zephaniah is the ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets and one of the last voices before the Babylonian crisis broke; Jeremiah, whose call came in Josiah's thirteenth year (Jeremiah 1:2), and Habakkuk worked in the same generation or just after. It stands between the prophets of the Assyrian period and those of the return from exile (Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi). Its announcement of the Day of the LORD develops a theme from Amos, Isaiah, and Joel, and its vision of the nations calling on the LORD's name with pure lips reverses the scattering of languages at Babel (Genesis 11). Josiah's reform delayed but did not prevent the judgment Zephaniah announced; within a generation of his death, Jerusalem fell to Babylon.
christ: Zephaniah does not name a coming Messiah, but its themes run into the New Testament. The Day of the LORD, a day of wrath and salvation, becomes in the New Testament the day of the Lord Jesus Christ, when he will return to judge and to save (1 Thessalonians 5:2, 2 Peter 3:10). The promise of a people from many nations calling on the name of the LORD with purified lips finds a fulfillment in Pentecost and the mission to the nations, and Paul's statement that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved (Romans 10:13, from Joel 2:32) belongs to the same hope. The call to the Daughter of Zion to rejoice because her King is among her (3:14-15) echoes in Zechariah 9:9, which the Gospels apply to Jesus' entry into Jerusalem. And the picture of God rejoicing over his people with singing anticipates Jesus' parables of the joy of heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15).
reading: Zephaniah is prophetic poetry with three main movements: judgment on Judah and the world, judgment on the nations, and judgment followed by restoration. Watch the repeated phrase the Day of the LORD and the related phrases on that day and at that time. Read the harsh opening in light of the tender ending; the book is designed to move from one to the other. A common misreading takes the Day of the LORD as purely a future end-of-the-world event; in Zephaniah it refers to God's decisive intervention, which fell on Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC and which also points to a final day of judgment. Another misreading hears the closing song as a comfort cut loose from the call to humility and repentance that comes before it.

structure.title: Heading
structure.summary: The word of the LORD to Zephaniah, a descendant of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah.

structure.title: The Day of the LORD against Judah and the world
structure.summary: God announces universal judgment, focused on Jerusalem's idolatry, violence, and complacency, and describes the great day of wrath.

structure.title: Seek the LORD
structure.summary: A call to the humble of the land to seek the LORD, righteousness, and humility before the day arrives.

structure.title: Judgment on the nations
structure.summary: Oracles against Philistia, Moab and Ammon, Cush, and Assyria, with promises that Judah's remnant will possess their lands and the nations will worship the LORD.

structure.title: Woe to Jerusalem
structure.summary: The rebellious city's leaders are condemned, and God's righteous presence in her is contrasted with her refusal of correction.

structure.title: A purified people and a rejoicing God
structure.summary: God promises pure lips for the peoples, a humble remnant in Zion, and a song in which he rejoices over his people and gathers the scattered.

themes.title: The Day of the LORD
themes.body: Zephaniah gives the Bible's fullest description of the Day of the LORD, the time when God acts decisively to judge sin and set the world right. It is near, it is universal, and it falls first on God's own people. It is a day of darkness for the proud and complacent, but beyond it lies salvation for the humble.

themes.title: Complacency and pride
themes.body: Zephaniah condemns those who say in their hearts that the LORD will do nothing, good or bad, and the carefree city that says it alone exists. The book treats practical atheism and self-sufficiency as the root of Judah's and the nations' sin.

themes.title: The humble remnant
themes.body: Those who will be sheltered on the day of the LORD are the humble of the earth, who seek righteousness and humility. God will leave a meek and humble people who trust in his name. Humility, not power or status, marks God's people.

themes.title: God among his people
themes.body: The LORD is righteous within Jerusalem even in its corruption (3:5), and in the restoration he is the King among his people who rejoices over them (3:15-17). His presence is both the ground of judgment and the source of joy.

themes.title: The nations brought to worship
themes.body: Judgment falls on the nations, yet the book promises that the nations of every shore will bow to the LORD and that he will give the peoples pure lips to call on his name. God's purpose reaches beyond Israel to the whole world.

keyChapters.why: The Bible's most concentrated description of the Day of the LORD, set against the idolatry and complacency of Jerusalem in Josiah's early reign.
The call to seek the LORD and humility, followed by judgment on the nations around Judah, shows both the reach of God's justice and the way of refuge.
The movement from woe on Jerusalem to the song of God rejoicing over his people is one of the great turns in the prophets.
